linux.fallback: constrained: only local filesystem types on the allow-list are searched and every other mount is reported by its own row; names compare byte for byte; a directory the agent cannot search is a gap, and the capability that lets the agent search directories of other accounts is held on the walking thread only around directory opens, directory listings and the leaf open (hygiene, not a boundary); the verdict reads partial when any mount, directory or name was not searched
linux.mechanism: resumable sorted depth-first search of the requested root, one slice per call, through no-follow directory opens; the mount table from /proc/<pid>/mountinfo decides which mounts are searched; the extents of every matched regular file from FIEMAP; matched files are opened and never read

macos.fallback: constrained: names compare by Unicode normalisation and case folding whatever the volume's own rule, so a case-sensitive volume can over-match; folders protected by the system's privacy controls are permission-denied gaps; a search rooted at / reaches the data volume through its firmlinks and reads partial; the verdict reads partial when any mount, directory or name was not searched
macos.mechanism: resumable sorted depth-first search of the requested root, one slice per call, through no-follow directory opens; the mount table from getmntinfo_r_np decides which mounts are searched; the extents of every matched regular file from F_LOG2PHYS_EXT; dataless files are never materialised; matched files are opened and never read

windows.fallback: not read yet: one unsupported status row, windows:planned
windows.mechanism: NTFS volume search and a directory walk with the same rows

caveats: **Windows is planned.** The Windows leg reads nothing and answers `status|search|unsupported|windows:planned`; a later change adds an NTFS volume search and a directory walk with the same rows. The descriptor and the capability matrix already declare all three legs.

**A search from `/` reads partial.** Every refused mount is a gap, so a search rooted at `/` cannot read `complete` on a host that has a pseudo, memory or network mount; narrow the root to read `complete`. On macOS the data volume is searched only through the system volume's firmlinks, so a data-volume directory that no firmlink exposes is not searched and the data volume's own row reads `partial` (`firmlinks_only`). From `/` every other APFS mount under `/System/Volumes` is its own unit, and where the update mount is present system files are reported again under it (pairing a snapshot with its base volume is tracked in #8454). A host that mounts a btrfs top-level subvolume also reads partial through `other_device` gaps on that mount.

**Only part of what changes between slices is seen.** The limits under "A search of more than one slice is not a snapshot" apply to every search that needs a cursor, and matches beyond the per-directory cap of one slice are not reported: that directory is named by a `match_cap` gap and the verdict reads partial, so a very broad pattern in one directory reads partial.

**macOS name matching and permissions are approximate.** A case-sensitive volume over-matches because names are compared case-insensitively whatever the volume says. Folders protected by the system's privacy controls are `permission_denied` gaps, a dataless directory is a `dataless` gap, and the behaviour of a daemon that holds no Full Disk Access over protected folders has not been measured.

**On Linux the capability scope is hygiene, not a boundary.** The packaged unit already gives the agent `CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH` for every plugin, so this plugin adds no grant and no packaging change. The search worker thread drops the bit from its effective set and raises it only around lookups, but the bit stays permitted on the thread, so code running on it could raise it, and every other thread of the agent holds it effective. Scoping it agent-wide is tracked in #8398. In the agent container image the agent runs as an unprivileged account with no capability (the image sets none). Adding the capability to the container is necessary but not sufficient for that account: it reaches only the bounding set, so a root container or an ambient grant is needed as well; otherwise the raise does nothing and the directories the account cannot search are `permission_denied` gaps. In the stock image the container's own root is an overlay mount, which the plan refuses (`fstype_not_allowed`), so only allow-listed host filesystems mounted into the container are searched; the single-file mounts a container runtime adds (the hosts, hostname and resolver files) are planned as units too, and each ends in a gap, so the verdict reads `partial`.

definitions.description: Searches the local disks of a device, under one absolute root, for files or directories whose name matches a leaf-name pattern, and reports each match with its type, size, modification time and the extents of the file. Names, types, sizes, times and extents are all that is returned: matched files are opened and never read, and no hash of anything is taken. One call is one slice of the search; repeat the call with the cursor row of the previous answer until a slice answers without one. Every answer ends with a search row stating whether the slice ran, and a coverage row stating whether everything under the root was searched, so an empty result is never confusable with a failed or partial one. Only local filesystem types on the allow-list are searched; every other mount under the root is named by its own volume row with the reason. A search of more than one slice is not a snapshot. Off until enabled; a non-administrator also needs an approval. What is stored is readable only with Forensics:Read. The Windows leg is planned and answers one unsupported status row.

description: On-demand, resumable search of the local disks by file or directory name, with the extents of every matched file; names, types, sizes, times and extents only
how_it_works:
`search` finds files or directories by leaf name under one absolute root on the local disks of one device. Each match is reported with its type, size, modification time and, for a regular file, its extents (where on the volume the filesystem keeps the file's data). The plugin reads names, types, sizes, times and extents. It never reads the contents of a file and takes no hash of anything. A matched regular file is opened read-only, without following a link, so the system can be asked for its size, time and extents; no byte of it is read, and an on-access scanner on the host sees the open. A matched directory carries no size, time or extents. Nothing is written, signalled or changed.

One call is one slice of the search. A slice ends when the walk finishes, or when it reaches a time, entry, row or byte budget, or when the search reaches its slice maximum (the budgets are named constants in the source and are not restated here). The slice's byte budget is sized against the server's default cap on stored rows per command and agent, `--response-max-rows-per-agent` (`YUZU_RESPONSE_MAX_ROWS_PER_AGENT`): a server set much lower can drop a slice's rows at the store, counted on `yuzu_server_response_ingest_dropped_total{reason=per_agent_cap}`. Every slice ends with exactly one `search` row. A slice that stopped early also writes a `cursor` row; the caller repeats the call with that token as `cursor` until a slice answers without one. The agent spends about half of each slice working and does not pace the caller: a loop that repeats the call with no pause keeps one device at that duty for the whole search, and on Linux the idle I/O class a worker asks for is a request the block scheduler may not honour. A search roots at one directory but may cross several mounts: each searched mount is one unit and a slice searches one unit, the mount that contains the root first and the others in order of mount point. Within a unit the walk is depth-first and visits the names of each directory in byte order. Every answer carries a `coverage` row that says whether everything under the root was searched, so an empty result is never confusable with a failed or partial one.

### The request

| Parameter | Rule |
|---|---|
| `root` | Mandatory and absolute. A trailing slash is ignored and `/` is the whole filesystem. An empty path, a doubled slash, a `.` or `..` component and a NUL byte are refused (`missing_root`, `root_not_absolute`, `root_too_long`, `root_bad_component`). On the first slice the leg checks the root itself: a root that is a link at any component answers `root_is_link`, one that does not exist `root_not_found`, one that is not a directory `root_not_a_directory`. The three tokens are the whole answer: nothing is searched. On macOS `/tmp`, `/var` and `/etc` are links, so those roots answer `root_is_link`; search `/private/tmp`, `/private/var` and `/private/etc` instead. |
| `pattern` | Mandatory. A leaf-name glob matched against each entry's name, never the whole path: `*` matches any run of bytes including none, `?` matches one UTF-8 character (one byte where the bytes at that position are not well-formed UTF-8), and every other byte, `[` and `]` included, is a literal. There is no regex, no character class and no escape; `/` and NUL are refused. A pattern that could match nearly everything is refused with its own token rather than run: too long (`pattern_too_long`), too many `*` (`pattern_too_many_stars`, each `*` of a run counts) or too few literal bytes (`pattern_too_few_literals`, a literal is any byte other than `*` and `?`). |
| `kinds` | `files` (the default), `directories` or `both`. |
| `cursor` | The token of the `cursor` row of the previous slice of this same search; empty for the first slice. A cursor is valid only in the agent process that issued it, for this root, pattern and kinds: a token the agent did not issue (made up, edited, from another query (root, pattern or kinds) or another device) and any token from before an agent restart is refused with `bad_cursor` before anything is read, and the search starts again without one. |

The pattern dialect differs from `device.filesystem.search_dir` in three ways: there is no regex mode and `[` and `]` are literals where `search_dir`'s glob reads a character class; the bounds above refuse a pattern `search_dir` would accept; and names are compared by the rule of the OS the agent runs on (next section), where `search_dir` compares the bytes of the name it is given on every OS.

### What a name is compared as

On Linux names compare byte for byte: case-sensitive, no normalisation. On macOS the pattern and every candidate name are normalised to Unicode form C and case-folded (CoreFoundation; ASCII is folded inline) before they are compared, whatever the volume's own rule: a case-sensitive volume is still compared case-insensitively, so two names that differ only in case both match. A macOS name that is not well-formed UTF-8 compares as the bytes it is. The `search` row states the rule that ran: `bytes` on Linux, `macos_nfc_casefold_v1` on macOS.

A name longer than 255 bytes cannot be placed in a cursor position, so it is not searched: it appears as a `name_too_long` gap. A filesystem that allows longer names (the HFS family counts 255 UTF-16 units, which can be more bytes) can hold such names. A name whose compared form is too long to match is the same gap.

### What is searched, and what is not

Only mounts of a local filesystem type on an exact, case-sensitive allow-list are walked: `ext2`, `ext3`, `ext4`, `xfs`, `btrfs`, `zfs`, `f2fs`, `apfs` and `hfs` (the list also carries the Windows volume-type names, which neither mount table reports). Every other mount at or under the root, or containing it, is not walked and is named by its own `volume` row with `not_searched` and the reason:

| Reason | Mount |
|---|---|
| `network_mount` | a network, cluster or paravirtualised type (NFS, SMB, FUSE network types and the like) and an `autofs` trigger point |
| `private_namespace` | a `/tmp` or `/var/tmp` that a service manager bound in from a private per-service directory |
| `fstype_not_allowed` | any other type: memory and pseudo filesystems (`tmpfs`, `proc`, `sysfs`, `devfs`), `overlay`, `squashfs`, `fuse` and `fuseblk`, FAT, exFAT and NTFS as the Linux and macOS tables name them |
| `behind_network_mount` | an allow-listed disk mounted beneath a network mount: reaching it would open a directory on that mount |
| `duplicate_mount` | a second mount of the same subtree (same device label and same root inside the filesystem); one is walked, the other is named |
| `firmlinks_only` | macOS, a root of `/`: the data volume (`/System/Volumes/Data`), which the system volume reaches through its firmlinks; the row reads `partial` |

A mount of another refused type that lies above an allow-listed disk (a `tmpfs` or `overlay` with an ext4 disk mounted inside it) does not block the disk: the walk crosses it with one no-follow open per directory and never lists it. A network mount above a disk does block it, because listing or opening on that mount can hang. These are deliberate exclusions, not omissions: a search does not touch a mount that was in the mount table when the slice began and may hang, never enters a link, and never lists a memory or pseudo filesystem; whether `tmpfs` belongs on the allow-list is an open decision (#8399). The mount table is read once per slice, so a mount made under a searched directory after that read is not in the plan and the walk can open it: it opens and lists the directory before it compares devices, discards what it listed and records an `other_device` gap (a different device is not walked), and if the open or the listing never returns the worker is abandoned and the volume reads stalled ("A volume that stalls"). The next slice reads the table again and prunes that mount. Refusing such a mount at open time is tracked in #8442.

Each unit's walk never enters, lists or names another mount point below it: the plan's `volume` rows are the one record of a pruned mount. So a mount point's own directory name is never a match candidate, and a directory bind-mounted at a second path (same device label, different root inside the filesystem) is a separate unit and is reported at both paths. Links are never followed and never matched; each one seen is counted in `links_skipped` on the `search` row. Entries that are neither a file, a directory nor a link (a FIFO, a socket, a device node) are never opened and never matched.

A search rooted at `/` reads `partial`, and says so on every slice, wherever a refused mount sits under it: every refused mount counts as a gap, and the verdict reads partial for anything not searched. On a typical Linux host that is the pseudo and memory filesystems; on macOS it is the data volume's own row and any mount of another type. A narrower root that holds no refused mount can read `complete`.

### Identity, extents and what a row can say

The match row carries `<device>:<file id>` in 16 hex digits each (the `extents` row names the same key). The device part is the number the system reports for the directory the entry was listed from, and the file id is the inode or file id. Identity is only as stable as the filesystem makes it: a remount can change a device number, a filesystem may reuse a file id after a deletion, and btrfs reports one device number per subvolume, so a nested subvolume that is not mounted reads as another device and is not entered (an `other_device` gap). A subvolume mounted at its own mount point is its own unit and is searched from there.

The `extents` row lists, for each file, up to a named cap of extents as `<logical>:<physical>:<length>:<flags>` and then the count, an exact number or a lower bound (`>=<n>`) where the system cannot count without listing. The offsets are the numbers the filesystem reports and what they are offsets into depends on it (a block device, a btrfs logical address space, an APFS container); the `btrfs_logical` flag marks the one case the leg can name. On Linux the request is `FS_IOC_FIEMAP` with no flags, so a file with data not yet allocated shows a `delalloc` extent with no physical offset, and the sync flag, which writes dirty pages back, is never used: a search never causes a write. A filesystem without the interface answers `unsupported`. On macOS the request is `F_LOG2PHYS_EXT` in pieces: a device offset of -1 is an `unallocated` hole, a file the filesystem keeps compressed answers `compressed` (with no extents), and `shared` is set on every extent of a file that shares all of its blocks with another (a clone) and on no other. A hole in a sparse file is listed and counted on macOS and not listed on Linux, so the same sparse file reads fewer extents on Linux. A file that cannot be opened for its facts is still reported, with size and time `-` and the extents state `failed`; a macOS file that is not present locally (dataless) is never downloaded to answer.

### Users' directories

A match whose path is a user profile directory, or below one, carries `user` in its last column; every other match carries `system`. The rule is on the path: on Linux `/home/<name>` and `/root`, and `/var/home/<name>` and `/var/roothome` (the spellings an image-based system uses, where `/home` is a link the walk never follows); on macOS `/Users/<name>` except `/Users/Shared`, and `/private/var/root`, each also when it is reached below `/System/Volumes/Data`. A home relocated elsewhere, or spelled in another letter case, is not tagged, so the tag is not a complete answer to "which rows are about a person"; it exists so an export can drop the rows it knows are. User directories are always searched: a root of `/` lists names under every user's home.

### A search of more than one slice is not a snapshot

The coverage row reads `consistency=single_pass` for a search that finished in one slice and `consistency=not_a_snapshot` otherwise. A later slice resumes by name and by the identity of the directories on the resume path, so a change between slices that moves neither is not seen and leaves no gap: an entry added at or before the resume point of a directory that kept its identity, a completed directory swapped for another of the same name, and a replacement that reports the same identity as the directory it replaced (a filesystem may reuse one) or differs from it only in the half (device or file id) the earlier record left unreported. Entries missed that way are not visited. A directory that changed identity is searched again from its start, so a match can repeat; it is never silently skipped.

### A volume that stalls

A slice that has not returned by its deadline plus a grace period leaves its worker running, blocked inside one system call, which the agent cannot cancel (a mount made under a searched directory after the slice read the mount table can cause it: see "What is searched, and what is not"). The agent records that volume as stalled in memory, in this agent process only, and any slice that reaches it answers a `stalled` `volume` row, counts one gap and moves on to the next volume without walking. When the blocked worker returns the entry is dropped by the next slice and the volume is searched again; nothing needs to be cleared by an operator. An agent restart also clears it: the agent keeps no state across a restart, so a volume that is still dead costs the next slice one more timeout. An agent stop or reconnect waits for a running slice: up to the slice time plus the grace period when its worker is blocked (tracked in #8353). With two workers still blocked every call answers `busy` until one returns or the agent restarts. The count of non-advancing attempts on one cursor is held the same way and starts again after a restart. A restart also ends every search in progress on that device: a cursor is valid only in the agent process that issued it, so the next call with an earlier cursor answers `bad_cursor` and the search starts again without one.

The runbook: the search is read-only; the agent keeps no state across restarts, and a cursor does not survive one; if a slice answers without a cursor and with a retryable reason (`timed_out`, `rejected`, `no_progress`, `internal_error`), repeat the call with the previous cursor, a bounded number of times, unless the agent has restarted since it was issued (the call then answers `bad_cursor`: start the search again); without a cursor, `stalled` and `unstable` are final.

### Who can run it and who can read the results

The catalogue row is `FileRetrieval` · Read · risk High · `AdminOrApproval`: an administrator can launch a search; anyone else needs an approval. Each slice is its own dispatch, so a caller who is not an administrator needs an approval for every slice of a search, not one for the whole search. It is not single-target, so a search can be sent to a group or the fleet. The plugin ships off: the server seeds a default-off kill switch, and an operator enables it with `PUT /api/v1/plugin-config/file_search/kill-switch {"enabled":true}`.

What a search stores is a different matter from who may launch it. The stored rows are Forensics-tier: only a caller holding a global `Forensics:Read` reads them (the Administrator and ForensicsAnalyst roles by default, and Administrator only while RBAC is off), and each read is audited as `response.forensics.read`. A non-administrator who launches a search under an approval therefore cannot read its results unless they also hold `Forensics:Read`. There is no second tier and no second permission check for this plugin; the rule is the one in `docs/authz-model.md` section 4.

Names compare by the rule of the agent's OS: byte for byte on Linux; on macOS normalised to NFC and case-folded whatever the volume's own rule.

name: file_search

columns.description: Row shape discriminator (field 0). Values: match, extents, volume, gap, gaps_dropped, volumes_dropped, coverage, cursor, search (the last row of every slice), and status (one row on a leg that is planned and not read yet).
columns.name: row_kind

columns.description: match: the path, with each byte outside well-formed printable UTF-8 and each % | \ written as %XX. extents: the file identity, device:file id in 16 hex digits each, equal to field 3 of the match row of the same file. volume: the mount point, escaped like a path. gap: the path of the directory or entry that was not searched. gaps_dropped and volumes_dropped: how many were left out of the answer. coverage: complete or partial. cursor: the token to pass back as the cursor parameter. search: ok, invalid, busy or failed. status: the literal "search".
columns.name: field_1

columns.description: match: file or directory. extents: ok, compressed (the filesystem keeps the file encoded and reports no extents), unsupported or failed. volume: the filesystem type. gap: the cause (depth, dir_unreadable, dir_truncated, other_device, network_mount, memory_cap, permission_denied, dataless, private_namespace, name_too_long, match_cap). coverage: slices=<n>, the slices of this search so far. search: the reason, a closed token (none, a coverage reason, a fault such as busy or timed_out, or a request error such as bad_kinds). status: unsupported.
columns.name: field_2

columns.description: match: the file identity, device:file id in 16 hex digits each, or "-" when unknown; the key of the extents row. extents: the extent count, or >=<n> when the system cannot count without listing. volume: complete, partial or not_searched. coverage: prior_gaps=<n>, gaps carried from earlier slices. search: the name rule that ran (bytes on Linux, macos_nfc_casefold_v1 on macOS), or "-" when no pattern was compiled. status: the planned token such as windows:planned.
columns.name: field_3

columns.description: match: the size in bytes, or "-" for a directory or a file that could not be opened. extents: the extents, each logical:physical:length:flags joined by commas, or "-" for none; flags are resident, delalloc, shared, compressed, encrypted, unwritten, unallocated and btrfs_logical joined by +, or "-". volume: the reason the volume was not fully searched (none, budget_entries, budget_time, budget_rows, cancelled, fstype_not_allowed, network_mount, mount_table_unreadable, permission_denied, private_namespace, other_device, stalled, unstable, unsupported, duplicate_mount, behind_network_mount, max_slices, mount_table_changed, firmlinks_only). coverage: consistency=single_pass or not_a_snapshot. search: seq=<n>, the slice number.
columns.name: field_4

columns.description: match: the modification time in seconds since the epoch, or "-" when unknown. volume: extents=collected, not_collected or unsupported, whether the matches on this volume carry extents. search: q=<8 hex>, a short name for this query that reveals neither the pattern nor the root.
columns.name: field_5

columns.description: match: system, or user for a path under a user profile directory (a rule on the path, so a home relocated elsewhere is not tagged). volume: entries=<n>, the entries visited on the volume. search: links_skipped=<n>, links seen and never followed.
columns.name: field_6

outputs_note: Every row is one line of `|`-separated columns, and `row_kind` (field 0) names its shape. A name or path in any column is written with each byte outside well-formed printable UTF-8, and each `%`, `|` and `\`, as `%XX`, so a column never holds the delimiter. Row grammars by `row_kind`: `match|<path>|<file or directory>|<device:id or ->|<size or ->|<mtime or ->|<system or user>`, `extents|<device:id>|<state>|<count>|<list or ->`, `volume|<mount>|<fstype>|<complete, partial or not_searched>|<reason>|extents=<collected, not_collected or unsupported>|entries=<n>`, `gap|<path>|<cause>`, `gaps_dropped|<n>`, `volumes_dropped|<n>`, `coverage|<complete or partial>|slices=<n>|prior_gaps=<n>|consistency=<single_pass or not_a_snapshot>`, `cursor|<token>` and `search|<ok, invalid, busy or failed>|<reason>|<name rule or ->|seq=<n>|q=<8 hex>|links_skipped=<n>`. On a leg that is not read yet the answer is the one row `status|search|unsupported|windows:planned`. Matches and their `extents` rows come first, then the `volume`, `gap` and `coverage` rows, then the `cursor` row when one is issued, and last the `search` row. The `volume` and `gap` rows describe the slice that wrote them; the verdict on the `coverage` row is cumulative across slices. A search with no match is the `volume` and `coverage` rows and the `search` row, never an empty answer. The `q` value names a search without revealing its pattern or root.

result_status.when: The slice ran, no cursor remains and the coverage verdict is `complete`: every volume was searched in full and there is no gap
The slice ran and either a cursor continues the search or the verdict reads `partial` (a refused or stalled volume, a gap, a dropped volume)
Another search slice holds the agent's one slot, or two blocked workers are still recorded; repeat the call
The request was refused (the command also returns 1); the `search` row says `invalid` and nothing was searched
The slice or the search ended without a result for that reason; the `search` row says `failed`
The body threw: one `search|failed|internal_error` row and the command returns 0

The leg reads nothing (caveat 1): one `status|search|unsupported|<os>:planned` row. `macos:planned` and `linux:planned` are the shared reporter's tokens and are not emitted by this plugin's POSIX legs

where_the_data_goes: **Instruction result.** Every row is server instruction-result data under the Forensics read tier: stored under the standard response retention and served over REST `/api/responses` and MCP only to a caller who holds a global `Forensics:Read` (Administrator and ForensicsAnalyst by default; Administrator only while RBAC is off). The live output events never carry these rows.

**Not consumed by** the daily sync, Echo or DEX: the action runs on demand only. Eight counters (`slices`, `budget_stops`, `stalled`, `unstable`, `timed_out`, `rejected`, `failed` and `gaps`, each a total since the agent started) are published as heartbeat status tags `yuzu.plugin.file_search.<counter>`; they carry no path, pattern or root. A log line names a search by the `q` prefix and a reason, never a path or pattern.

**Default off, and how to turn it on.** The server seeds a default-off kill switch at boot, so nothing dispatches until an operator runs `PUT /api/v1/plugin-config/file_search/kill-switch {"enabled":true}` (`PluginConfig:Write`, audited as `plugin_config.kill_switch.set`). Launch is then `FileRetrieval` with `AdminOrApproval`.

**Sensitivity.** Rows list the names of files and directories under every directory searched, including other accounts' profile directories, with sizes, modification times and the physical layout of each file. Names can identify a person (a profile directory carries an account name, and a file name can name a document or a client) and the listing is reconnaissance material about what a machine holds. A match under a profile directory is tagged `user` so an export can drop it; a relocated home is not tagged. No file content and no hash appears in any row. The committed sample was taken over a scratch tree.

**Siblings:** `device.filesystem.search_dir` (names under a confined root, glob or regex, no extents), `device.filesystem.find_by_hash` (matches by content hash), `crossplatform.components.scan` (installed components) and `crossplatform.storage.mounts` (the mount inventory).
